newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa may get World Bank industry loan in rand.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa may get World Bank industry loan in rand.

text.p: The World Bank said on Tuesday that it may take the unusual step of denominating a development loan to South Africa in rand rather than a more usual currency such as U.S. dollars or Deutsche marks.
South Africa is talking to the bank about a loan to fund a Department of Trade and Industry scheme to boost the competitiveness of its small- and medium-sized businesses.
World Bank country director Pamela Cox said giving a loan in rand would be highly unusual, but that it was willing to consider the scheme.
"We are very open to the suggestion," she told reporters.
"We have never done this sort of financial product before...however, we have assured the government we will look at the possibility."

With the current weakness of the rand a loan taken out in stronger currencies could prove expensive. Cox said it was up to the South African government to cost the measure and then decide which currency it wanted.
"Goverment has to look to see if it is cheaper in rand or a foreign currency," she said.
Talks on the loan are still in the pre-appraisal stage and no exact sum has been fixed, but a figure between $35-60 million is the most likely, Cox said.

Yvonne Tsikata, World bank task manager for the loan, said its final structure should be proposed some time next month. "In the next couple of weeks we will have a better idea of the design," she said.
World Bank representatives praised the government's economic plans, in particular the macro-economic strategy announced by finance minister Trevor Manuel In June this year.
The plan, stocked full of market-friendly policies, aims to double annual growth to six percent and create 400,000 new jobs a year by 2000.
"It is a sound macro-economic strategy. It is fiscally conservative, it is trying to address the development issues," Cox said.
But the African National Congress-led government's perceived closeness to international financial institutions has aroused suspiscion among its labour and communist allies.
When the World Bank's sister organisation, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), visited the country recently it earned condemnation and protests by Cosatu, South Africa's biggest labour group.

Cox said there needed to be more understanding of the World Bank's policies. "The most important thing is that if people feel they want to demonstrate they should demonstrate, but let's have a discussion about the issues," she said.

Washington-based Cox is also country head for Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland. She had just completed her first World Bank trip to South Africa and met with officials and non-governmental organisations.
She said no meetings had been arranged with labour unions, but that plans were afoot to include them on her next trip in two months time.
